clinicalPearls: Caused by absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel, producing a tonically contracted, non-relaxing aganglionic segment and functional obstruction.
Most neonates present with delayed passage of meconium beyond 48 hours, abdominal distension, and bilious vomiting.
The aganglionic segment extends proximally from the anus for a variable distance; short-segment disease confined to the rectosigmoid is most common and it is more frequent in boys.
Associated with Down syndrome and other congenital conditions, and there can be a positive family history.
Contrast enema may show a transition zone between the narrow distal aganglionic bowel and dilated proximal colon, but a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis.
Anorectal manometry shows failure of the internal anal sphincter to relax with rectal distension.
Rectal suction biopsy demonstrating absent ganglion cells with hypertrophied nerve trunks is the diagnostic gold standard.
Definitive treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic segment with a pull-through procedure connecting normally innervated bowel to the anus.
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis is the most serious complication and can present with fever, distension, foul explosive diarrhoea, and sepsis.
reference.pathophysiology: Failure of the craniocaudal migration of neural crest-derived enteric ganglion cells leaves the distal bowel without submucosal (Meissner) and myenteric (Auerbach) plexuses. The aganglionic segment cannot relax and remains tonically contracted, while abnormal cholinergic and other innervation adds to the dysmotility. This creates a functional obstruction with proximal dilatation (megacolon) and predisposes to stasis, bacterial overgrowth, and enterocolitis.
additionalDifferentials: Meconium plug syndrome / small left colon syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Rectal suction biopsy for absence of ganglion cells (with acetylcholinesterase staining or calretinin)
Contrast (unprepped) enema to identify a transition zone
Abdominal radiograph showing distal obstruction with dilated proximal bowel
Genetic and syndrome evaluation where relevant
redFlags: Failure to pass meconium within the first 48 hours of life
Fever, explosive foul diarrhoea, and distension suggesting enterocolitis
Signs of sepsis, dehydration, or shock
reference.prognosis: After definitive pull-through surgery most children do well, though some have ongoing issues such as constipation, soiling, or recurrent enterocolitis; outcome is worse with long-segment or total colonic aganglionosis and with severe enterocolitis.
pitfalls: Attributing neonatal obstruction solely to functional constipation and missing aganglionosis
Relying on a normal contrast enema to exclude the diagnosis
Overlooking Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis, which can be rapidly fatal
Taking a biopsy too close to the anal verge where ganglion cells are normally sparse
Missing associated syndromes such as trisomy 21
management: Definitive surgical pull-through resecting the aganglionic segment (Swenson, Soave or Duhamel procedure)
Preoperative decompression with rectal irrigations and washouts, occasionally a levelling colostomy, to relieve the functional obstruction
Prompt recognition and treatment of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis with washouts and antibiotics
Postoperative bowel management for persistent constipation or soiling using laxatives, enemas and routine washouts
Internal-sphincter botulinum toxin for postoperative obstructive symptoms from a non-relaxing sphincter
Genetic evaluation and counselling given RET associations and the link with Down syndrome
Multidisciplinary paediatric surgical, continence and nutritional follow-up
